title: The Principles of Training
description: Specificity, overload, reversibility, variance and individual needs; how FITT helps coaches design effective programmes.
content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Any training programme can make an athlete fitter — for a while. But without a structured framework, progress stalls, performance peaks prematurely, or the athlete risks injury through poorly judged workloads. The principles of training give coaches a shared language and a set of rules to design programmes that produce genuine, lasting gains. Each principle addresses a different risk: specificity guards against wasted effort, overload drives adaptation, reversibility reminds us that fitness is temporary, variance keeps athletes engaged, and individual needs ensure the programme fits the person, not just the sport.

Specificity

Specificity states that the body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed upon it. A long-distance runner who only does weight training will develop muscular strength but will not improve cardiovascular endurance — they have trained the wrong system. A coach applying specificity asks: What energy systems does this sport primarily use? What muscle groups are most important? What movement patterns must be replicated? A basketball coach, for example, would design drills involving explosive lateral movements, short sprints and jumping — not long, steady-state running — because those match the physiological and technical demands of the game. Specificity also applies to position: a goalkeeper's training programme will differ markedly from a midfielder's even within the same sport.

Progressive Overload

The body adapts to a given training load and then reaches a plateau. To keep improving, the load must be progressively increased — this is progressive overload. Overload means working at a level above what the body is accustomed to; progressive means the increase is gradual and planned rather than sudden. A swimmer who completes 20 lengths per session without discomfort must eventually swim 22, then 24 lengths to continue improving. If the overload is too rapid, the risk of injury rises sharply; if it is absent, fitness stagnates. Progressive overload is the engine of fitness improvement and is closely linked to the FITT principle, which gives coaches four specific handles to control the overload applied.

Key Fact

The FITT principle provides four variables a coach can manipulate to apply progressive overload: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), and Type (which training method). Increasing any one of these variables increases the training load on the athlete's body.

The FITT Principle

The FITT principle gives a coach four specific levers to increase training load in a controlled way. Frequency is how often an athlete trains — moving from three sessions a week to four increases the total weekly training stimulus. Intensity is how hard the athlete works — a runner increasing their average pace from 8 km/h to 9 km/h imposes a greater cardiovascular demand. Time refers to the duration of each session — extending a session from 30 minutes to 45 minutes adds volume. Type is the training method selected — switching from continuous running to interval training recruits the anaerobic energy system more heavily and creates a different physiological adaptation. Coaches rarely change all four variables simultaneously; instead, they adjust one or two each week or training block to ensure overload is applied safely and systematically.

Reversibility

Fitness is not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced, the body reverses its adaptations — cardiovascular endurance declines, muscle mass decreases and flexibility is lost. This is the principle of reversibility, sometimes described with the phrase "use it or lose it". Research suggests cardiovascular fitness begins to decline noticeably within two to three weeks of inactivity, while strength losses are slightly slower but still significant within four to six weeks. A coach managing a swimmer recovering from illness must plan a structured return to training, gradually rebuilding the load rather than expecting the athlete to resume immediately at their previous level. Reversibility also underlines the importance of rest and recovery being planned — complete rest for weeks at a time is rarely beneficial.

Key Fact

Reversibility means that fitness gains built through months of training can be lost within weeks if training stops. Cardiovascular endurance declines fastest — noticeable changes occur within two to three weeks — while strength takes slightly longer to reverse.

Variance (Tedium)

Repeating exactly the same sessions week after week causes two problems: physical plateauing, as the body adapts completely to a familiar stimulus, and psychological tedium, as athletes lose motivation through repetition. The principle of variance — sometimes called the principle of tedium — requires coaches to introduce variety into training to prevent both. A football coach might rotate between circuit training, fartlek running, small-sided games and plyometric sessions during a pre-season block. Varying the type of training also ensures that multiple components of fitness are developed — not just the one or two that appear in the regular session format. Importantly, variance should not mean randomness; sessions should still follow specificity and progressive overload principles — variety is introduced within a structured plan.

Individual Needs

No two athletes are identical. Their current fitness levels, injury history, age, gender, role in the sport, goals and available training time all differ. The principle of individual needs states that a training programme must be tailored to the specific performer, not applied generically. A 16-year-old beginner taking up rugby will require a very different programme from a 22-year-old experienced player preparing for a county trial — even if both play the same position. A coach who ignores individual needs risks under-challenging a fit athlete (who will plateau and become bored) or over-loading a less-fit one (who risks injury and burnout). Fitness testing data — gathered from tests such as the multistage fitness test or the Illinois agility run — gives a coach the objective baseline they need to set genuinely individual training loads.

Rest, Recovery and Applying the Principles

Progressive overload works only if adequate rest is built into the programme. During exercise, muscle fibres are stressed and micro-damaged; it is during recovery that the body repairs and strengthens these fibres, producing the adaptation that improves fitness. Without sufficient rest, the cumulative damage exceeds the body's repair capacity, leading to overtraining, fatigue and injury. A coach designing a weekly programme for a 100-metre sprinter might schedule three high-intensity sessions with rest or light activity days between them, allowing full neuromuscular recovery before the next intense stimulus. Rest is not wasted training time — it is when the adaptations triggered by overload actually take place. A well-designed programme applies all five principles together: it is specific to the sport, progressively overloaded via FITT, varied to maintain motivation, and tailored to the individual — with rest built in at every stage.

Imagine a coach preparing a recreational cyclist for a 10-week sportive ride. In week one, the athlete trains three times a week (frequency), at a moderate steady pace (intensity), for 40 minutes per session (time), using continuous cycling (type). By week six the coach has increased frequency to four sessions, pushed intensity into threshold pace for intervals, extended two sessions to 60 minutes, and introduced interval training to target the aerobic-anaerobic boundary. Each change is deliberate — only one or two FITT variables change in any given training block, so the coach can identify what is driving improvement and avoid over-loading the athlete. This systematic adjustment is exactly what the exam expects candidates to be able to describe and apply to a given scenario.

When training load is increased too sharply — more than roughly 10% per week as a general guideline — the cumulative stress on muscles, tendons and bones exceeds the body's ability to repair itself. The result is overtraining syndrome: persistent fatigue, declining performance, irritability, suppressed immune function and a significantly elevated injury risk. Common overtraining injuries include stress fractures, tendinopathy and muscle strains. This is why progressive overload must be gradual and why rest days are non-negotiable components of any well-designed programme. A good coach monitors signs of overtraining (flat performance, low mood, disturbed sleep) and is prepared to reduce load — temporarily applying the principle of reversibility deliberately to allow full recovery.
exam_tip_html: In applied-scenario questions, always link the principle to the specific sport or performer described. Writing "the coach should use progressive overload" scores 1 mark; writing "the coach should gradually increase the number of interval reps each week to ensure the sprinter's anaerobic system is continually challenged" scores 2 or 3 marks. For FITT questions, name all four components, define each briefly, then give a sport-specific example of how each could be increased. In extended responses, show that the principles work together — specificity directs what to overload, FITT controls how to overload it, variance prevents plateauing, and individual needs determines the starting point for each athlete.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Specificity means training must match the demands of the sport and the athlete's role — the right energy systems, muscles and movement patterns must be targeted.
  • Progressive overload drives adaptation: the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) gives coaches four variables to increase training load in a controlled, systematic way.
  • Reversibility reminds coaches that fitness is temporary — two to three weeks of inactivity causes measurable cardiovascular decline, so return-to-training plans must rebuild load gradually.
  • Variance prevents physical plateaus and psychological tedium by rotating training methods, while individual needs ensures the programme is tailored to the specific athlete rather than applied generically.
  • Rest and recovery are not optional extras — adaptation occurs during recovery, and insufficient rest leads to overtraining, declining performance and increased injury risk.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the principle of specificity?
A) Training load must be increased gradually over time
B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role
C) Different training sessions should be used to prevent boredom
D) Each athlete requires a different amount of rest between sessions
practice_questions.marks: B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the four components of the FITT principle.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct components: Frequency / Intensity / Time / Type. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the principle of reversibility and give one sporting example of when it would apply.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): reversibility is the loss of fitness adaptations when training is reduced or stopped. Explanation (1 mark): e.g. the body no longer needs to maintain the higher fitness level so cardiovascular endurance, strength and flexibility decline. Sporting example (1 mark): e.g. a swimmer who is ill for three weeks will return to training with a noticeably lower aerobic capacity and will need to rebuild their programme gradually. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A coach is planning a ten-week training programme for a 16-year-old club tennis player who currently trains twice a week for 30 minutes. Describe how the coach could use the FITT principle to apply progressive overload over the ten weeks.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks — one mark per FITT component correctly applied with an appropriate progression example: Frequency (e.g. increase from 2 to 3 sessions per week by week 5); Intensity (e.g. introduce high-intensity drills and reduce rest periods between rallies); Time (e.g. extend sessions from 30 to 45 minutes); Type (e.g. add in agility ladder work and plyometric drills alongside court-based practice). Answers that simply name the four components without applying them score a maximum of 2 marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A football coach has been running the same three sessions every week for the past two months. Several players have reported feeling bored and their fitness test scores have stopped improving.

Discuss how applying the principles of training could address these problems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least three principles with clear application to the scenario. For example: the plateau in fitness scores indicates that progressive overload has not been applied — the coach should increase frequency, intensity, time or type using the FITT principle to provide a new stimulus. The player boredom reflects a failure to apply variance — rotating between circuit training, fartlek sessions and small-sided games would reduce tedium and maintain motivation. Individual needs should also be considered — some players may have plateaued because the current sessions are too easy for their fitness level while others are struggling.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two principles identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One principle identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sprint athlete has been training consistently for six months and has improved their 60-metre time from 8.4 seconds to 7.9 seconds. They then sustain a soft-tissue injury and are advised to rest completely for four weeks.

Evaluate the likely impact of this rest period on the athlete's fitness, and explain how the coach should plan the return to training using the principles of training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Reversibility correctly applied — cardiovascular endurance declines within 2-3 weeks; neuromuscular adaptations (speed, power) also diminish; four weeks of complete rest means a significant reduction in anaerobic capacity and fast-twitch muscle conditioning. Return-to-training plan uses multiple principles: individual needs (assess current fitness before resuming, not assuming previous level); progressive overload via FITT (begin at reduced intensity and duration, gradually rebuilding over 2-4 weeks); specificity (sprint-specific work — acceleration drills and block starts — reintroduced progressively); variance (initial sessions may include cross-training to maintain general fitness without stressing the injury site before full sprint training resumes); rest and recovery (adequate recovery between sessions to allow tissue repair). A substantiated judgement — e.g. the reversal of six months' gains within four weeks highlights why managing return-to-training systematically is critical, and why coaches must monitor fitness test scores post-return rather than assuming full recovery.
Secure (5-6 marks): Reversibility explained and return plan covers at least two principles applied to the scenario.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points mostly descriptive with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which principle of training states that the body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed upon it, meaning training must match the demands of the sport?
The FITT principle identifies four variables a coach can manipulate to apply progressive overload. Which of the following correctly names all four?
The principle of _____ means that fitness adaptations are lost when training stops or is significantly reduced, as the body no longer needs to maintain the higher level of conditioning.
Introducing variety into a training programme to prevent physical plateauing and psychological boredom is an application of the principle of _____.
Match each principle of training to the correct description.
right: The programme must be tailored to the specific athlete's fitness level, role and goals rather than applied generically
Training must target the correct energy systems, muscles and movement patterns for the sport and athlete's position
Gradually increasing the training demand so the body is continually challenged beyond its current level

flashcard_questions.q: What does the principle of specificity mean for a coach planning a programme?
flashcard_questions.a: Training must target the correct energy systems, muscles and movement patterns for the sport and athlete's role.
Gradually increasing training demands so the body is continually challenged and forced to adapt.

flashcard_questions.q: What do the letters FITT stand for?
flashcard_questions.a: Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type of training.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a coach use the Frequency component of FITT to apply overload?
flashcard_questions.a: By increasing the number of training sessions per week to add more training stimulus.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Intensity component of FITT refer to?
flashcard_questions.a: How hard the athlete works during a session, such as pace, weight lifted or heart rate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the principle of reversibility?
flashcard_questions.a: Fitness adaptations are lost when training stops, as the body no longer needs to maintain that level of conditioning.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how quickly does cardiovascular fitness begin to decline noticeably when training stops?
flashcard_questions.a: Within two to three weeks of inactivity.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is variance included as a principle of training?
flashcard_questions.a: To prevent physical plateauing and psychological tedium caused by repeating identical sessions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the principle of individual needs require a coach to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Tailor the programme to the specific athlete's fitness level, age, role and goals.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is rest and recovery an essential part of any training programme?
flashcard_questions.a: Adaptations occur during recovery; without rest, cumulative damage leads to overtraining and injury.

flashcard_questions.q: How does FITT relate to progressive overload?
flashcard_questions.a: FITT gives coaches four specific variables to increase training load in a controlled, systematic way.

flashcard_questions.q: What risk arises if training load is increased too rapidly without adequate rest?
flashcard_questions.a: Overtraining syndrome: persistent fatigue, declining performance and elevated injury risk.

glossary_terms.definition: A set of guidelines that underpin the design of any effective training programme, ensuring it produces real, lasting improvements in fitness.
Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's specific role within it, so that adaptations occur in the right muscles, energy systems and movement patterns.
Gradually increasing the demands of training over time so that the body is continually challenged and forced to adapt beyond its current level of fitness.
A framework for applying progressive overload by adjusting four variables: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type of training.
The loss of fitness adaptations that occurs when training is reduced or stopped entirely, as the body no longer needs to maintain the higher level of conditioning.
